maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW EXPORT CONTROL LIST

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW EXPORT CONTROL LIST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an announcement to make with regard to the Canadian export control list. By order in council P.C. 1958-1158 of August 15, 1958, a new export control list is established, effective from August 16. This will be published in an early issue of the Canada Gazette, perhaps the August 27 issue. I have here copies of the revised export control list which I will table for the information of hon. members.
In revising our export control list in conformity with the agreed new strategic list, it has been the objective wherever possible to narrow the range of commodities of all types which will require export permits. As a result, in many cases items which remain under control have had to be defined in greater detail. Although the effect at first glance at the list disguises the real extent to which the list has been narrowed, examination will show that there have been very significant changes in the content of the list as far as Canadian export trade is concerned. Such items as aluminum, copper, and many forms of nickel have been dropped from control, as have a number of items of metalworking machinery, general industrial equipment, electronic equipment, transportation equipment and chemical products. The revised list will include as new items certain electronic devices, jet fuels, containers for liquid gases, and certain chemicals.
Many of the items which have been dropped from the list in all likelihood will find no place in our exports to Soviet bloc destinations. The most significant effect of removal of control in these cases is that permits will no longer be required for exports to friendly countries. The export control list, moreover, serves an important function in indicating those items which are regarded as strategic, and an endeavour has been made to set forth the list in such form that traders may use it for this purpose. This means that if items are not on the export control list, permits will be readily available for export to any Soviet bloc destination on application. Permits
for all exports to Soviet bloc destinations will still be required under our general area control of shipments to such destinations.
It is our purpose in administering export controls to reduce the paper work for all concerned to the essential minimum, and to eliminate misunderstanding. Our new export control list will serve as a clear lead as to strategic control policy. We are prepared to discuss with exporters ways and means by which we can still further simplify for them the procedure in complying with the remaining controls. Special permits can be used for regular shipments of items on the export control list to specified destinations, and further general permits for specified goods to destinations subject to area control. These possibilities will be given continuing attention in the department, and exporters are invited to indicate their interests. Our objective is a major reduction in the necessity for individual licences.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW EXPORT CONTROL LIST
speechtext: In connection with a statement the minister has just made, may I ask whether when he uses the expression "Soviet bloc countries" he includes continental China in that group, and if not whether there is a special list for continental China?

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW EXPORT CONTROL LIST

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEVELOPMENTS AT UN SPECIAL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a number of hon.
TMr. Churchill.]
members have asked me respecting the major developments which have taken place during the emergency special session of the general assembly up to the time of its adjournment yesterday.
President Eisenhower, in his statesmanlike speech, made a number of points which deserve the close attention of all members of the United Nations. Among those points was the emphasis which he placed on the need for the economic development of the area in the Middle East and the need to have the function of leadership invested in the Arab states themselves. Similarly, in the suggestions he made for a United Nations body to examine the question of the flow of heavy armament to the nations of the Middle East, he stressed that any arrangements made in this connection must reflect the views of the countries of the region.
The President made a number of other suggestions in which Canada has a continuing interest and which are now undergoing thorough study.
One of the suggestions made by the President, that for a stand-by United Nations peace force, is of course of particular importance and interest to Canada, because we have consistently advocated the need for flexible United Nations machinery which can be employed to prevent dangerous international situations from developing into international hostilities. We hope the present crisis in the Middle East will focus the attention of members of the United Nations on the necessity for taking steps so the United Nations can quickly and effectively deal with threats to any country's independence and integrity, not only to restore order once hostilities have broken out but to prevent armed conflict from breaking out at all.
The points made by the President that I have mentioned so far relate to long-term problems in the area which may require extensive consideration and detailed preparation, because they are essentially regional problems. There are, of course, more immediate problems in the area demanding early solution. President Eisenhower referred to these as well in his references to United Nations concern for Lebanon and to the need for United Nations measures to preserve peace in Jordan. The United Kingdom foreign secretary and others have also dealt in preliminary fashion with the issues involved. However, the statement of the Jordanian delegate on Thursday to the effect that Jordan did not wish to have either United Nations observers or a United Nations force on its territory has introduced a new and unexpected element, requiring careful examination in the light of further information that may become available. The Jordanian

authorities have not, however, ruled out some form of UN representation appropriate to the situation in their country.
The task now, as we see it, would be to attempt to develop solutions to these problems in an atmosphere of mutual co-operation and restraint. I am sure the house will agree that this process will not be facilitated by too many public utterances or the taking of firm positions. I would hope that all those countries directly concerned would exercise moderation and forethought in anything they may say or do in the circumstances.
I think it is only fair to say that Canadians as a whole will be very pleased that during the last few days at the United Nations it has been generally recognized that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) has played a full and important part in these important negotiations.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEVELOPMENTS AT UN SPECIAL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house I know will have heard with great interest the Prime Minister's statement on the important developments taking place at the United Nations assembly in New York. I do not wish to add to any public statements that are being made, but I should like to state my agreement with what the Prime Minister has said to the effect that the original statement of the President of the United States was hopeful in the sense that it seemed to put forward ideas which might serve as a basis for a resolution providing for United Nations action in the Middle East which might help to solve some of these problems. This action, however, if it is to be effective will have to include the participation of all the leading members of the United Nations.
As the Prime Minister has said, the reaction of the representative of Jordan in his original statement was discouraging. I sincerely hope it will be possible for the Jordanian government to alter the position which it seems to have taken in this statement and which is very difficult to understand coming from a country whose stability is now being protected by the troops of the United Kingdom.
It is difficult to understand why a country in that position should hesitate to accept replacement by a kind of international intervention which would make possible the withdrawal of the United Kingdom troops. We must hope that that position can be altered.
I would like also to assure the Prime Minister that we all, without regard to party, are happy about the activities of the Canadian delegation. We know that under the leadership of the Secretary of State for External Affairs they will play a useful and constructive part in those developments.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in the C.C.F. are pleased with the hopeful indications from the United Nations that this very grave problem may be solved. We feel that our stand in past weeks, when we said that United States and United Kingdom troops should not have gone into that area and should subsequently have been withdrawn, has proven to be correct.
We were pleased with the statement by the President of the United States. We hope it may be possible to establish United Nations forces or United Nations observer teams in that area which will replace the troops from outside nations who are now stationed there. We further hope that this will be accompanied by a large-scale economic development program, always bearing in mind the interests of the citizens of that area.
I have read with approval the press reports of the decision taken by the Canadian delegation at the United Nations. I agree with the Leader of the Opposition that the stand taken by Jordan is most disturbing. I have also read with concern reports of the position being taken by the United Kingdom and the great reluctance to withdraw her troops from Jordan. In spite of the position taken by the United Kingdom, I hope Canada will press forward on a middle course, designed to bring peace to that area. Since we are a very important and prominent member of the commonwealth, we may exert over the United Kingdom that influence necessary to bring the United Kingdom and the United States into agreement, together, we hope, with other major powers, so that peace will be restored and maintained in that area.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of Ihe Opposition):
subtopic: VISITS TO NORTHERN DEFENCE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of National Defence. In view of the fact that a spokesman for the United States state department appears to have contradicted a statement made in this house by a minister on the subject, will the Minister of National Defence state what exactly are the procedures which must be observed by Canadians, whether members of the government, officials or non-officials, visiting United States or joint United States-Canadian defence installations in the Canadian Arctic?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: VISITS TO NORTHERN DEFENCE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, possibly I could
answer that question. Throughout the years I have felt that in the northern defences of Canada there were in existence situations that could conceivably derogate from Canada's sovereignty. When I became Prime Minister one of my first acts was to have this question looked into in detail, with a view to assuring that, while we co-operate in defence willingly and freely, in no way shall our sovereignty be impeded or interfered with; and further than that, that everything that could possibly be done should be done to assure that our sovereignty to the North pole be asserted, and continually asserted, by Canada. Following that viewpoint, as I said, negotiations have taken place. As was said by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, as appears at page 3542 of Hansard, a friendly and favourable response has been the result of the representations made.
The most recent outline of agreed procedures is contained in the agreement arrived at in respect of the distant early warning line and the co-ordinating committee in that behalf. This co-ordinating committee was established some years ago to provide for interdepartmental consultation on the technical problems arising from the construction and operation of the D.E.W. line. Procedures in effect are today visit reporting procedures and not clearance procedures, and in effect are arrangements that were required purely for administrative reasons.
[Mr. Nowlan.l
The facilities of the distant early warning line are relatively spartan. Advance knowledge of visitors is essential if food and lodging is to be made available. For that reason agreements have been reached by which in the planning and arrangement for the provision of accommodation at stations, account has to be taken of the indicated requirements for limited transient accommodation in order to look after the departmental personnel whose presence at the site is necessary in connection with the performance of their official duties. No provision has been made in the construction of the stations for the accommodation or feeding of personnel except those associated with the operation of the line or whose presence is necessary because of the construction and operation of the line. There are particular provisions in respect of civil air carriers which are not applicable to the question asked by the hon. gentleman.
Today the situation is that all that is required is that departmental personnel, government representatives and the like who desire to travel in the area shall make known their intentions, to the end that the D.E.W. line co-ordinator, Department of National Defence at Ottawa, may make the necessary representations to the areas in question to provide not only for stopovers, if stopovers are necessary, but also for refueling facilities.
I am glad to say that as a result of the representations we made changes have been effected. The other day the Leader of the Opposition made it quite clear that he realized that there had been regulations during the time he administered the department of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. These requirements have gradually, in the light of mutual discussions, been amended, and today there is nothing that requires to be done that in any way interferes with, impedes or diminishes our sovereignty.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED ENTRY OF UNDESIRABLE PERSONS FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of her known aversion to the entry into Canada of gangsters, thugs and racketeers from the United States, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. In view of the fact that police authorities in Montreal are reported as saying that shady characters from the United States have a lot to do with the terrific rise in the crime level, and in view of the law in this respect, can the minister explain why these persons are permitted to enter Canada and, in view of the fact that the Canadian people are banking on departmental courage in facing this problem, would the minister inform the house what action is taken by the officials of her department to prevent the entry or the continued residence in Canada of these undesirable characters?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: REPORTED ENTRY OF UNDESIRABLE PERSONS FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I read the article in this morning's press, and I am sure we all regret it if the statement is true. However, I inquired in my department, as well as I could on a Saturday morning, and I could find no trace of the department having been approached by the police of Montreal for assistance in this regard.
The United States-Canadian border is probably the most open border in the world. We are very proud to have a great many United States tourists visit Canada every year, and we are also glad that our people are very easily able to go into the United States. I may say we have no specific figures with regard to border crossings, but an estimate for 1957 was that some 53 million people crossed the border from the United States into Canada.
Obviously we could not examine every one of those persons. It is a matter for the local police to ascertain if they have in their community people who are objectionable, and I can assure the hon. member that upon application from any municipal authority which can supply us with the information required, my department will not hesitate to take such action as may be necessary to remove objectionable persons from this country.

an honest living so they can provide their families with the necessities of life. The Canadian worker does not want charity or a dole. The Canadian worker simply wants employment. It is the duty of this government to provide him with an opportunity to work. We all remember very well a few months ago when hon. gentlemen opposite in the Conservative party were going all across the country and from both sides of their big mouths were promising that everyone in this country would have work. It is about time something was done about it.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as a member representing a large number of industrial workers I wish to take advantage of this opportunity to make a few brief comments on several matters that concern the working people of my constituency. I might explain before proceeding that as an honorary member of a trade union and as a small employer and as a farmer-

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: As everything.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
-who has lived in complete independence all his life slightly above the parish relief level, I am able to take a strictly objective view of this question.
While we know that on the whole the labour movement in Canada is democratic in structure and controlled by the rank and file, there are a few blotches on the escutcheon that are causing serious concern to many of the rank and file members of the trade union movement in this country, to the public in general and to hon. members of this house. From my experience in interviews with trade unionists, from correspondence I have received from the Atlantic to the Pacific and from a large number of interior places, and from numerous affidavits I have received in recent months which for the first time have been forthcoming from union members, I am of the opinion, as are some other hon. members who have expressed themselves previously in this debate, that there is an unhealthy state of affairs in a few trade unions in this country.
To illustrate that point I mention the fact that just prior to dissolution last session two members of the seamen's union came to this house and spoke for nearly three hours to 25 members of parliament representing all parties. I can tell you that from their point of view it was a hair-raising experience.
Personally I have received many complaints from workers on pipe lines, and I investigate them to the best of my ability. Prior to coming to Ottawa last session I discovered that an American was in charge of one operation and was collecting union 
dues, and the poor beggars who were paying the dues did not know what union they belonged to. They never saw a business agent or attended a meeting, and often after paying $15 for dues they would be fired three days later and other chaps hired.
A good many hon. members of this house were concerned recently by newspaper reports stating that a Canadian union critic of Mr. Hoffa, who was secretary of one of the largest teamsters' unions in Toronto, was fired by Mr. Hoffa. These things are not being taken very well by the rank and file of labour, the Canadian people or a large number of members of parliament.
In every case brought to my attention these violators of the democratic rights of Canadian workers and the principles of union democracy were imports from the United States. Just as I resent any control of the Canadian economy by large United States firms, in the same way I resent any interference with Canadian union affairs on the part of people like Mr. Hoffa and his associates. I trust, Mr. Chairman, the day will not come when that type of person and others associated with him are able to control the organized labour that will be related to the operation of the St. Lawrence seaway.
I know it is the responsibility of the Canadian labour movement to deal effectively with those who violate the traditional principles, practices and procedures of the movement. I wish to say most emphatically, and I say it without any fear or hesitation, that the rank and file of labour in Canada, the Canadian people and this parliament expect the senior officials of the Canadian labour movement to accept their responsibility in this respect.
To illustrate a different state of affairs from the one or two isolated illustrations I have given that are causing concern, I mention the fact that just prior to coming to Ottawa this year I called a conference of all the trade unions in Kootenay East and Kootenay West, which was attended by representatives from the railroaders, carpenters, plumbers, electricians, I.W.A., mine-mill and all the rest. I wanted to find out what labour was thinking. I wanted to acquaint myself with the present opinions of labour with respect to federal legislation and the problems we have to face here. It was a most successful meeting indeed, the best labour conference we have ever had in the district.
The acting president of the Nelson and Trail district labour council was elected chairman of the meeting and the secretary of the largest local of mine-mill, No. 480 at Trail, was elected secretary. We had a discussion with the rank and file with various members getting up and fiercely expressing their criticism on certain matters, advancing their

opinions with respect to legislation and also expressing their attitude regarding local, national and international affairs. I am one of those who all through his life has had a great deal of confidence in the rank and file of any organization. It has always been a treat for me to meet with these union men. Those are the people I deal with, and I have found that whenever you deal with the rank and file and place the facts before them you need have no fear as to their acceptance of responsibility with respect to any decision they may make.
I just mention that to illustrate what can be done in a very small sphere. These unions, representative of all types of labour, repeatedly have taken part in local affairs on the municipal level or community level or on the regional level with respect to the hospital building, community planning and things of that kind, and they have made a most valuable, constructive and responsible contribution to the development of public affairs in my district. I look forward to the time when the rank and file of the labour movement in Canada will participate across this country in just as effective a way in expressing their opinions with respect to local, national and international problems.
I have said these few words on a matter about which I am seriously concerned and I am always given to speaking my mind, Mr. Chairman. Never in my whole life has anyone stopped me from saying what I thought to be right, proper and correct, on any question.
I listened to the minister's opening remarks with interest, and I must say that we all like the minister. You know, he has that common touch that removes the latent fear in the hearts of some members of parliament when they approach persons in the seats of the mighty. You can go to the minister's office and you can discuss any problem that concerns you. I want to say that as one member of this house I appreciate his approach to members and his willingness to discuss a problem, no matter how insignificant it may be from the national point of view. I think it is only fair to express my appreciation in that respect, and I know that other members in this group think of him in the same way.
I was glad that in his opening speech the minister suggested that amendments to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act were being considered. I think it is a growing conviction that, in view of changing conditions, the development of large-scale industry, as mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition, and the consequent natural development of large-scale unions on the other side, a national labour code is required to indicate clearly the responsibility of the employers to
Supply-Labour
the community as a whole and the responsibility of larger unions to the community as a whole and their responsibility to the rank and file of the working people of this country. I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that with the co-operation of the labour movement such an act can be drafted to meet the circumstances that exist today and protect the basic rights of the Canadian working people.
I was also pleased to hear the minister speak of a proposed consultative committee on employment practices. I trust this is another step forward toward the banishment of discrimination and unfairness in employment in this country. I am very happy to say, so far as my experience has been, that this is lessening very rapidly from day to day. It is a very different world we are living in today from the world of 1906. I remember the general election in 1906 when the slogan of the Tory party was, "A white B.C.; keep the oriental out." We have all learned a lot. Mind you, in fairness to them I might say that quite a number of labour organizations at the time had an identical attitude toward life. We have progressed a good way in that direction, and all that is required now is to remove those few little blemishes here and there where we find they exist.
I am glad the minister is taking further steps in that direction. I am pleased to hear of the addition to the staff of the civilian rehabilitation branch. This should in some measure increase the effectiveness of that branch, which is doing very good work indeed. Also, the minister's proposals to increase the employment of older persons are particularly welcomed by this group. I know this is a very difficult problem, because I meet it from day to day when I am in my constituency.
This is a problem of serious concern to the persons directly affected and to many other persons who have their welfare in mind. So many good Canadians are still able to make a worth-while and constructive contribution to the productivity of this country or to the services of this country but are denied the opportunity because of the difficulties that have developed as a result of automation and the development of our mechanized and industrial society. Anything the minister can do in that respect will be heartily welcomed by this group.
I was also pleased to see in the estimates and to hear the minister's statement that there will be an increased expenditure for vocational training. That is very necessary indeed. In fact I think it is an urgent matter, because while old chaps like me now on the slippery slope of life with their heels dug in hoping to avert the inevitable as long as

Supply-Labour
possible should not be worried too much, I do like to see opportunities provided for thousands and thousands of young Canadians who are possibly in some instances not suited for or do not prefer academic or professional life, but who provide a great pool of young, virile people who will in the future provide the artisans so badly required in Canada for the development of our natural resources, transportation, communications, and our industrial structure. I do hope that the increase in the estimate in this respect will continue from session to session.
While I am on that point may I say I am not given normally to speaking on the parochial level, but I must use this strictly as an illustration. There is great need of a vocational school to serve the southern interior of British Columbia, particularly the Kootenays, where we have had a very rapid expansion of the smelting, mining and lumbering industries. There we have, I know personally, hundreds of young people who are not going to university, are not going to take higher education, and who would love to have an opportunity to take vocational or trade training in vocational school at some reasonable distance from their homes, where they could undertake it without unnecessary cost and so on.
I understand those vocational training schools are established as the result of action by the provincial government, which makes application to the federal government for assistance in those expenditures in that respect. I do hope that when the minister replies to the comments made by members in this debate he will inform us a little more as to the procedure with respect to the application of this vocational training estimate, because I have a good number of people in my constituency in all walks of life who are very concerned with the fact that we have these young people leaving school. If they are taken at the right time and given vocational or trade training they can make a great contribution to Canada. If the vital two or three years are overlooked and missed, then they go on into blind-alley occupations and we fail to take advantage of those human resources as we should.
I do not want to detain the committee too long but I have one or two other remarks to make. I have often wondered why there was duplication of employment services with the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. For instance, I found an officer of the national employment service-and they are hard-working people in my constituency- trying to get jobs with the lumber companies for some applicants for employment. They happened to come to the company
[Mr. Herridge.l
with which I am associated, and the next day an immigration officer turned up. He wanted us to employ some immigrant.
To me this seems a duplication, and I am of the opinion that it entails an unnecessary expense at times, and also there is certain irritation if an official of one department has been in and scoured around and done his best to find employment for those who are applying for employment, and then an official from another department arrives two or three days later on the same mission but on behalf of another branch. It seems rather odd to people in the community, especially the employers. I should like the minister to express his views on this and see whether something cannot be done to avoid what appears to me and to a good number of other people to be a somewhat unnecessary duplication.
I also want to mention very briefly something which came up at the conference where they discussed all these problems. I find the great bulk of the industrial workers are very concerned about the early establishment of a national pension scheme by this government in order to provide security so far as pension rights are concerned and mobility of employment, which I think is the right of every Canadian under present conditions. I do hope the minister will say a few words on this question and let us go away with a sort of hope in our hearts that something is going to happen in that respect at the next session of parliament.
I now come to my concluding remarks, and I have really evaporated most of the water out of what I had to say in order to save time. I find that unemployment is a major concern of a large number of people in my constituency, and I am sure it is a major concern all across the country, not only of those who are unemployed but of those who possibly fear unemployment. With so much to be done in this country with respect to national development, development of transportation, of highways, of parks and of things of that sort, it seems wasteful and sinful to let Canadians remain idle while this work has to be done.
I am not underestimating the difficulties. It is quite easy to rise on the opposition side and make all sorts of grand proposals. As the chairman knows, I always try to keep my feet on the ground. However, I suggest that there is here an opportunity for cooperation between the federal government and the provincial governments in some basic planning so that this winter we can utilize, as far as is humanly possible, this good investment even if we have to go into debt to do it. If we had gone into debt during the depression to build highways and to build

houses, we would have built them much more cheaply than we are building them today. That lack of foresight and fear of the future with respect to overexpenditure does not now exist because of our experience during the war and post-war periods.
I urge the minister to urge upon his associates the necessity for some approach to the provinces in order to see whether something cannot be done to plan this type of work across this country. I can think of dozens of places in my constituency where for years people have been driving around dangerous bluffs a thousand feet above a lake on a 16 foot road with no guard rail. That is the type of work that can be done in the winter economically and properly by persons who would otherwise be unemployed, such as miners, men who work in the woods at high levels who are laid off, and persons of that sort. I urge the minister to give consideration to this matter and to have a word or two to say on what he has in mind when he replies to the various members who have spoken.
My concluding point is this. The other day when I was speaking, I think it was on the agricultural estimates, I urged the Minister of Agriculture to do what he could to get the Minister of Labour to include in new amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act farm workers or farm employees. The present circumstances are most unfair to the men and women who are willing to go and work on farms, usually at lesser wages; but they are persons of the type who, if the circumstances are at all right, would prefer to work on a farm rather than work in industry. Yet because they are willing to do that they are denied the protection which other workers get under the Unemployment Insurance Act. This situation is not fair to the workers concerned, and it is not fair to the farmers who are obliged to employ these people. I urge the minister to give consideration to that matter. I trust that the pleadings of the Minister of Agriculture will meet with a favourable response in the heart of the Minister of Labour.
Those are the few things I have to say at this time, Mr. Chairman. I shall anticipate with great pleasure, hope and confidence the reply the minister makes to the various comments hon. members have made in this debate.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
I shall be very brief, Mr. Chairman. There are one or two points which I think should be made at this time and which have not yet been made. I would urge the minister to give serious consideration to bringing farm labour under the benefits
Supply-Labour
of the unemployment insurance legislation. Farmers are having difficulty in getting the help necessary to do their work. At the same time we know there is some unemployment in our towns and cities. However, there is little inducement for workers to take temporary jobs on farms when by so doing they will not add to the time they can use in applying for unemployment insurance benefits. There is a great deal of temporary work on our farms such as fruit picking, tobacco work, work in the beet fields. I feel that it would help both the farmers and the unemployed if these benefits can be extended to farm labour.
There is another point that I feel should be made at this time. In making it I should like to make clear first of all that I believe in organized labour. I believe that organized labour is doing a good job in this country. I believe that the aims, objectives and aspirations of organized labour should be protected in every reasonable way. But organized labour has become one of the most dominant forces if not the most dominant one in our economy. As such they must be prepared to accept their full share of responsibility for our national welfare.
The speech of the hon. member for Kootenay West this morning and that of the hon. member for Timiskaming yesterday are going to be of considerable value in making this point which I shall briefly mention. It has been suggested to the minister and to the government that they should use their influence to convince organized labour of three desirable policies. The first is that labour must not organize in such a way as to constitute a threat to the public control of our institutions. In that regard I took a Canadian Press clipping from the London Free Press dated August 13. It states:
President Claude Jodoin of the Canadian Labor Congress plans to convene a meeting of unions representing about 100,000 workers to try to work out a formula for avoiding clashes or organizing jurisdictions on the St. Lawrence Seaway.
The last paragraph of that article reads as follows:
The congress wants a wider representation, to take in unions covering all phases of seaway transportation.
I read that extract as an indication of the objectives of labour and in order to point out that the time has come when not only organized labour itself but all the people of this country should take a good look in order to see where organized labour is going. I can remember when in 1919 in the city of Winnipeg, in the course of the general strike there, organized labour were issuing permits for the delivery of milk. This procedure was

Supply-Labour
found to be a contravention of the civil authority and a number of people were sent to jail. I have been personally acquainted with some of those people, and I may say that they were very fine people. If organized labour and the people at that time had looked ahead and considered what were likely to be the results of some of the policies of labour in those days, that Winnipeg general strike and the unhappiness of those individuals could have been avoided. I think the time is ripe when the public of Canada and the government should take a new look at where the present policies of labour are likely to lead them.
The second policy is that labour must hold its share of the line against inflation. We know that there are strikes going on now. The steelworkers are asking for a 33 cents an hour increase, and even now they are getting almost double the wages that labour receives in the rural areas and the smaller towns of the constituency of Middlesex West. Labour must take its full share of the responsibility for what is likely to happen if these requests for large wage increases are enforced. We know what will happen; there will be another round of inflationary pressures in all respects, and nobody can win.
In the third place, I think the government should try to impress upon labour the fact that labour must not control the civil service, the police or other services vital to our national life. This is where the speeches by the hon. members for Kootenay West and Timiskaming were of great assistance. Those speeches pointed out in no uncertain terms that there are undesirable characteristics in some of the unions. In addition, there is a tendency on the part of unions in Canada to stay with their international affiliation. The hon. member for Timiskaming had this to say about the woodworkers' union of America, as reported at page 3633 of Hansard for August 15, 1958:
-the Canadian membership outnumbers and outranks the United States union membership but they have made no effort to change the structure in order to create a national union, which they could have done quite easily by a vote at any of their conventions. The Canadian union had a majority and could have seceded from the union and become a national union had they wished to do so, but there are many advantages to belonging to an international union.
The point I wish to make and impress upon the minister and the government, Mr. Chairman, is this. Canada cannot afford to have services vital to our national existence under the control of foreign labour bosses.

I should like to associate myself with the remarks made by my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate,

when he spoke about unemployment insurance and particularly unemployment amongst fishermen in Newfoundland. In my own riding, based upon recent visits to any number of smaller outports and upon fairly extensive correspondence, it would appear that perhaps more than 50 per cent of the fishermen who are recipients or those who should be recipients of unemployment insurance suffer from extended delays, partial payments and in some cases a complete lack of benefits which they really deserve. The result is that in some cases there is direct want, and in all cases embarrassment and dissatisfaction.
Perhaps one of the worst features of this is that the purpose of providing unemployment insurance for fishermen has not been fulfilled, that is putting fishermen on the same basis as the men who work in the fish plants and encouraging those who prefer to make fishing their vocation to do so. Last night it was stated by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that probably the remedy lay in the appointment of officials who would travel from place to place and advise the fishermen as to how they should make out their returns. These officials would, in turn, see the unemployment insurance officials and advise them as to what these recipients were entitled to. As I think the minister knows, the trouble in many cases lies in the fact that the original applications are not made out properly. It seems to me that the spirit of the act is not being carried out if some allowance and some provision is not made to ensure that these people, whom the act is designed to help, can receive their proper benefits.
I should like to suggest also that field men be appointed who would travel from out-port to outport advising the fishermen and generally acting as liaison officers between the department and the fishermen. This would enable the problems of the fishermen to be straightened out with a minimum of embarrassment to those people who should be helped.
I should like also to call to the minister's attention the fact that this year in Newfoundland we have had a very poor fishing season. It has been described as the worst in 25 years. Certainly it is the worst in recent years. The poor fishery, coupled with a cut back in woods operations because the paper companies are not cutting as much pulp this year, has made this a difficult period. Undoubtedly the coming winter in Newfoundland will be the worst in many years.
I would ask him, therefore, to use his influence with his colleagues to get some of the small works, such as wharves, breakwaters and so on-works which are already in the government's plans and for which surveys

have already been made-started. These works provide a considerable amount of local employment, and if he would endeavour to get them started they would be of considerable benefit. He might also consider having the federal government undertake the building of, say, a 100-mile section of the trans-Canada highway, which would provide additional employment. Certainly we are going to need that employment this year worse than we have for many years past, and worse, I hope, than we shall need it in the future.
In concluding these brief remarks I should like to pay tribute to the minister for the kind co-operation I have always received from him and his departmental officials. He has been able to infuse into the cold mechanics of official administration a kind of warmth which we appreciate.

I was not able to be in the house when the Minister of Labour made his opening statement, but I have read it carefully. The thing that seemed missing from his statement was any coming to grips with the present widespread unemployment in this country. I had hoped that by this time the government, which has now been in office for more than a year, would have enunciated and developed a program to deal with unemployment, the situation in respect of which is much worse than it was a year ago.
One would have expected that the government would be doing this because of the frequently repeated statements of the Minister of Labour, of his colleagues in the cabinet and of the Prime Minister himself that the Conservative party would lick the unemployment problem. They blamed the previous government last session and during both election campaigns for the conditions which then existed, but I do not think the government can now attribute the current widespread unemployment to the policies of the previous administration. Those policies may have been a contributing factor, but it is the policies of this government today which will decide whether or not we are to have anything approaching a state of full employment.
The feeling seems to be growing in Canada that labour has become irresponsible and that our great unions are acting in an irresponsible fashion by doing things which are against the general welfare of our country. I have not at any time changed my attitude toward labour; I have always felt and I have always said in this house that over the years Canadian labour has in general taken a highly responsible attitude, and that the policies followed by organized labour in Canada have not only contributed to an improvement in

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: It is easy to get up in this house and say, as has been said this morning by the hon. member for Middlesex West, that labour must be careful and must be cautious because it can add to the inflationary pressures in this country. It is easy to say that, but 1 think the government would be in a much stronger position when giving out this gratuitous advice to organized labour if it would put its own house in order. I ask to what extent is the government of this country presently adding to the costs-the real costs-of doing business and of living in Canada? Members on the government side of the house can say to labour "Don't rock the boat; don't ask for increases in wages", but how is labour going to pay the increased cost of buying a house, which situation has been directly brought about by the policy of this government in respect to increasing interest rates? This policy of increasing interest rates in its reconversion program is adding to the real cost of living of every Canadian family, because when interest rates go up, since they are a very important part of doing business, I think we all recognize that costs go up generally, because business will do its best to pass on those increased costs to the consumer.

I think I have the same right as every other member has to make a statement, and if the minister wishes to reply to me he may do so after I have sat down or, if other members wish to take part in this debate, at some later stage.
I was merely saying there seemed to be a growing feeling in certain quarters that strikes, when they occur in this country, should be looked at very carefully to see whether or not compulsory arbitration should be applied in their settlement. Without doubt, in certain industries if a strike should occur human lives might be endangered. The generation of electricity is one example, or the provision of gas in an area where people depend entirely on gas. If a strike were called, say, in the dead of winter, in temperatures of 20 or 30 degrees below zero, there is no question but that this would be the case, and in such circumstances any responsible government would have to consider taking steps toward settling such a strike as quickly as possible.
But I do think the record of this country as far as strikes is concerned is one that stands as an example to most of the nations of the world. We have in this country a labour movement which is responsible and which does not engage in long drawn out strikes which give Canada a bad name. That is not the situation at all. As a matter of fact the record of this country as far as time lost through strikes is concerned is excellent indeed.
I have in my hand a copy of the Labour Gazette dated July 31, 1958. These figures are given on a monthly basis, but for the months of January to May, 1957, the percentage of estimated working time lost through strikes was .05 to .08. In 1958, from January to May, the loss of time ranged from .07 to .18 per cent.
I have looked at the statistics back over the years, and generally speaking the amount of time lost through strikes and lockouts in this country amounts to approximately .1 per cent of the working time. If one assumes there

are five million workers in this country and that .1 per cent is the regular amount of loss, this would mean that on any given working day 5,000 workers are out on strike or are idle because they have been locked out; and when one compares the number of
5,000	on strike because of action they have themselves, taken, deliberately, with the figure of over 300,000 who are unemployed through no fault of their own, one sees that the problem of strikes in this country is not a particularly serious one for our nation; it has been magnified out of all proportion.
It may seem to us that an easy way, a short cut, to deal with strike situations is by compulsory arbitration, but one of the freedoms which Canadians have enjoyed for many years is the freedom to organize collectively in their own unions, and if they believe they have a just cause, to withdraw their labour. If we do not want this kind of freedom maintained, if we should wish to substitute for that freedom compulsory arbitration by multiplying its use many times, we shall be taking away a fundamental right of the Canadian working man; we shall be taking away a fundamental democratic right; we shall be acting in an un-Canadian and an undemocratic way.
I think compulsory arbitration, if it is proceeded with as a normal instrument of government policy, will add to the number of days lost and multiply the number of strikes in this country. This has been the experience in Australia and other countries where compulsory arbitration has been used as a general policy.
I had hoped, as I said at the outset, that the Minister of Labour would inform the committee of the policies the government is adopting to provide full employment and to restore employment. The goverment's attitude was very firm in this regard. The Montreal Gazette of March 20 contains an article which is headed "Job Policy Paid Off-Starr". The article has this to say:
.reaerai Labour Minister Michael Starr predicted last night the present unemployment situation will ena by mid-June.
He drew attention to the latest figures released by the dominion bureau of statistics showing a drop in the rate of unemployment.
"These figures are dropping faster than anticipated he said.
Mr. Starr, here to address a foreign language meeting of the Monument Nationale last night attributed the unemployment drop to the pump-pnming policies of the Diefenbaker government.
"We knew these policies would correct the situation, but we did not think the favourable results would be reflected so quickly", he said.
Does the minister feel now that he can take this kind of satisfaction that the unemployment situation has been corrected and

Supply-Labour
dealt with, in the light of the current situation? Does he think the pump-priming policies of the federal government, whatever that may mean, have been successful in dealing with this situation?
Of course the Minister of Labour is not the only one who has said that these policies were working. The Prime Minister, in a Canadian Press report which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of March 22, 1958, is reported as having said:
I hope that by June or July the application of our policies will have met the problem, through loosening tight money-
That is a very pertinent statement at this time, "through loosening tight money".
-and through public works, so that no one will be suffering from unemployment.
Seasonal benefits have been discontinued, unemployment is just as high now as it was a year ago, yet the Prime Minister said that by June or July the application of his policies would result in the situation being corrected.
I was present at a meeting held in the railway committee room toward the end of June attended by a delegation mainly of automobile workers from the city of Windsor and five or six cabinet ministers. Did these representatives feel at the end of June that the problem had been dealt with and the situation met? No; they said there was actual suffering in the city of Windsor because of unemployment.
It is easy to rise in this house and say labour is increasing the cost of production and the cost of living, that labour in the steel industry is receiving twice as much in the way of wages as labour in rural areas, but I believe the attitude of organized labour toward farmers is excellent. Canadian agricultural producers have today in the Canadian Labour Congress one of their very best friends.

Hon. members on the government side may snicker if they wish, but when the united automobile workers made their presentation at that meeting in June one of the points they emphasized in their brief was that it is necessary for the government to deal with agricultural income in such a way as to increase it. Organized labour participating in that meeting demonstrated something that we in this group have known to be correct for a long time; that you cannot have full employment in Canada when there is a depressed condition in agriculture. And so, far from attempting to drive a wedge between the farmer and labour, we feel both

organizations and the membership of both are good loyal Canadians who work hard for a living and are entitled to receive a reasonable wage for a reasonable day's work.
Following that meeting a conference was held in Ottawa in the early part of July under the sponsorship of the federal government and the Minister of Labour. At that conference were people representing organized labour and people representing business and management. We had hoped at that conference to deal with the question of seasonal unemployment. We had hoped that from that conference would emerge a program and policy that would prevent winter unemployment. The Minister of Labour promised to cure the problem of summer unemployment. The Prime Minister said that by June or July summer unemployment would not be with us. Well, the government failed to alleviate summer unemployment. Is the government now going to fail in the same way to prevent winter unemployment, which is a much more difficult problem to meet?
As I indicated, we had hoped a program of winter employment would be forthcoming from that conference. Immediately following the conference I questioned the Minister of Labour in this house as to whether a program had been agreed upon, and since that time various questions along the same line have been asked of him. The most recent information we have received is that the report is now in the hands of the Department of Labour. I do not wish to misquote the minister and he may correct me if I misinterpret what he said, but I understand the report is now being processed to the point where it can be turned over to the federal cabinet for consideration.
Does that represent progressive action? Does that indicate any great degree of speed in meeting the problem? Parliament is in session, but it may not be in session very much longer. At the rate the government is going I wonder if it will introduce a policy concerning winter employment that will assist to alleviate the situation this year.
I would hope the government has so crystallized a program to deal with and prevent winter unemployment that it will have concrete legislation to present at this session, but if the delay continues one will be led to ask whether it will be possible to deal with winter unemployment this year in an effective manner.
The minister referred to certain measures the government was considering. The government had a public information program. It sought to talk itself out of a winter recession

by advertising and giving advice to the building trades. That program cost $150,000. Looking over the main estimates I find there is less provision tor that kind of thing this year than there was last year. I hope this does not mean the program, which never has been adequate, is now being reduced. Rather I hope that this and other programs will be brought before parliament to deal with this situation.
According to one set of figures we have
300,000	unemployed. This is a serious matter for the Canadian economy. The number of unemployed at present is twice that of a year ago. Are we in a position either in the domestic field or internationally of being able to afford to have half a million unemployed in Canada again this winter? In all seriousness I ask the following question. How can we attract to the democratic world as supporters of our way of life the people of the uncommitted nations, people with a low standard of living, if they look to Canada and see all these idle resources?
The provision of full employment and full production is important to the economic standards of Canadians themselves, but it is also important in terms of Canada's stature in the world today. If we have solved the problem of unemployment and achieved full production we can say to the uncommitted nations of the world that our way of life is adequate; that we have been able to provide the man who wants a job and an income with a position and a wage. As I have said on another occasion in this house it is estimated that during the last 12 months Canada has lost production to the value of $1,500 million because of unemployment. That production could have been put to excellent use for the welfare of Canadians and as part of Canada's contribution to economic development in other parts of the world.

Mr. Chairman, I expect that my remarks will be quite brief at this time. First
Supply-Labour
of all, I want to thank all hon. members for participating in the debate on the first item of my estimates, and particularly for the worth-while suggestions that have been made as to how the functions of the department could be improved. To be fair in my remarks, I also wish to say I appreciate the criticisms that have been brought to our attention. Most certainly, a great many of those criticisms deserve to be looked at carefully to see where we can make some corrections that will bring about the kind of change in our department that will be of benefit to those who come under the laws and jurisdiction of the Department of Labour.
A number of questions have been asked regarding certain functions of our department and I would suggest that hon. members who have those questions in mind should ask them on the appropriate item of our estimates. However, I should like to make one or two observations, particularly to the hon. member for Dollard who advocated the introduction of legislation designed to abolish discrimination by employers against older workers in the matter of employment. He referred to the enactment of this type of legislation by a certain state legislature in the United States.
As I have said, Mr. Chairman, we are intensifying our work in relation to the employment problem of older workers because this has been a problem that has been foremost in my mind for a number of years now, since I have seen what is happening in the labour market as regards older workers. We propose to keep in touch with the operation of the United States legislation to which the hon. member has referred. This legislation is very recent and it will only be possible to determine its value and effectiveness by watching its operation. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that progress in meeting the problems of older workers will come mainly from the process of education, employment counselling, research and co-ordination of efforts of all agencies working in this field. I am quite willing to look at any proposal which will be effective in improving the lot of those older workers.
The Leader of the Opposition brought up the subject of automation and that, too, is a very important subject now and will be more so in the future. Automation, more properly referred to as technological changes of all kinds, is having an important effect on manpower requirements in industry. Many of the comments about those changes, however, are merely opinions or general impressions. The kind of technical changes occurring in industry and the ways in which those are altering requirements for different skills and training courses are a very complex matter. In this difficult area we need facts rather

Supply-Labour
than opinions and speculative suggestions. This is why our approach to this problem has been, first of ail, to find the facts. For the last year or so the Department of Labour has been carrying forward a number of research studies to learn more about those technological changes and their manpower and training implications. To help ensure that this research is keeping its feet on the ground, as it were, we have established an advisory committee composed of the representatives of organized labour, of industry and of our universities to advise and to comment on the work we are doing.
I do not want to leave the impression that the only action taken so far is research. The vocational training agreements now in existence with the provinces put special emphasis on the extension of training facilities for the type of workers so often referred to as technicians. We know that there is a growing need for workers with advanced technical training and we are therefore encouraging the provinces to expand those kinds of facilities.
As far as unemployment is concerned, I should like to leave my remarks on that aspect of the matter until we reach the item relating to unemployment insurance. With respect to the matters that were brought to my attention regarding unemployment insurance as it affects fishermen and various other aspects of these matters, I would prefer to make my remarks when we reach that item.

I am glad to note that the minister is now in a mood, as I would hope, to answer some of the questions I have

raised. I had said this morning also that there had been some substantial increases in the cost of living since this government took office. In view of these increases in the cost of living, it is understandable that the working people of this country are anxious that their real incomes should not be reduced by a continuing rise in the cost of living. The minister pointed out that there had been some levelling off in recent months. But I would point out to him that when the government took office in June, 1957 the consumer price index stood at 121.6 and that in June, 1958 the index stood at 125.1, an increase of 3.5. If the minister will check on the matter, I think he will find that that is the largest increase from June to June in many years. The previous June also saw a very substantial increase in the cost of living index but it was slightly less than 3.5, being 3.3. But the increase for a number of years was small in relation to this large increase that has taken place from June of 1957 to June of 1958.
A few moments ago, in speaking on the general subject of automation or technological change, as I believe he called it, the minister pointed out that this matter provides a certain real problem. Workers who are engaged in industry where technological improvement is going on at a very rapid rate and where therefore the workers' productivity is being increased at a rapid rate naturally feel that they should share in this increased productivity. I think that feeling applies to working people generally. I think it applies to the civil service of this country. When they see certain improvements by way of business machines being introduced or automation in the Post Office Department and so on, they naturally feel that they are entitled to an increase in their real incomes because of increased productivity.
Statistics show that an increase in the real productivity of this country can be or should be expected at the rate of 3 per cent per year. When one considers the increase in productivity and the large increase in the cost of living in the last year, he cannot help but have great sympathy for the civil service association of this country and the civil servants generally in asking that these two extremely important factors be considered by the government. As the minister has made reference to increased productivity, I think it is in order to make a reference to the position of civil servants.

We would be very glad to go on with a discussion of these estimates, and if the government would make up its mind in the meantime we could proceed on the first day the government did not have to make a motion to go into supply. In the interval the minister could make his report to the cabinet and then to the house on the occasion to which I have referred. The report on the winter employment program is what we want to debate and a discussion of it would not, I believe, be in order on any item of the estimates other than item No. 1 of the estimates of the Minister of Labour. It was in order to respect the desire of the

Supply-Labour
Minister of Labour to preserve the confidence that he is entitled to preserve until he has reported to his colleagues in order to let this government make up its mind, if it is capable of making up its mind, and to report to the house, that I made this very reasonable request, and I make it again.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
Order. The Chairman must insist once again on asking hon. members to respect standing order 59, subparagraph 2, which states clearly:
Speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
We are considering item No. 170 and we must confine our remarks to this item. Shall item 170 carry?

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a while ago I listened to the Minister of Public Works. He said that in the industrial relations committee nothing was said to indicate that any opposition came from there. I know that I for one accepted the report on division so that we could have a chance to study the matter in the house. Furthermore, the minister seems to think that the request of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is something extraordinary when he asks that item 170 stand and that we go ahead with the other items and come back to item 170 later on in order to give the minister a chance to report to the cabinet and be in a position to say whether there is really some legislation in mind to alleviate the hardship of unemployment.
When I was a member of the Quebec legislature-I do not know whether it is still the same today; there have been many changes since I left-item 1 of every department was allowed to stand until later in the session so that we could come back to it to deal with events that may have taken place during the session. It has been the common practice to follow that procedure in the Quebec legislature, and I do not see anything in the standing order, or in any of the practices of this house, which would prevent us from standing the first item and passing the remainder of the items and then coming back to the first item later after the minister has had a chance to discuss the matter with the cabinet to see whether any legislation really is in preparation to help in the unemployment problem of the coming winter. That is what we want and I do not think the Minister of Public Works has any right to make the remarks he made because I really believe they were the cheapest remarks ever made in this house.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
Earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said that he did not wish to anticipate government
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
legislation and he was right. He has been the clerk of the privy council and he knows very well that by this action in asking that this item stand he is using a form of blackmail.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have very rarely raised a question of personal privilege in this house but I believe blackmail is a crime and I believe it is contrary to the rules for one hon. member, even in jest, to suggest that another hon. member has committed a crime or is attempting to commit a crime. As a good lawyer I am sure the Minister of Public Works would be the first to agree with me in this. I must say that personally I could not care less about this charge because, as the Minister of Public Works has said, my life is an open book and I do not think anyone thinks I have ever indulged in the crime of blackmail. But I am speaking, sir, on a question of privilege. I do feel-

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: Sit down; the Chairman is on his feet.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: I would like to take advantage of the invitation of the Minister of Public Works to search for one of those 25 ways. I have been trying to track down what the 25 ways may be.
