speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope the minister will not think that I am attempting to hold up his estimates because that is the last thing I would want to do. I held a position similar to his and I know how much I became annoyed when, just at the time the item was about to pass, someone rose and made a speech which I thought was embarrassing. I did not like it. Therefore, I am going to do my best not to make an embarrassing speech and not to try in any way to hold up the minister's estimates; but I am prompted to rise because of the discussion that was originated earlier and because of a remark made by my genial friend across the way, the leader of the house. The fact is that he made a statement here which was quite at variance with one he made earlier in the session.
During the discussion of the motion to send many of these estimates to standing committees for consideration, the point was made that such procedure would not affect in any
Supply-Labour
way the discussion in the house. What is happening now is that after the estimates of this particular department, namely the Department of Labour, have gone to the standing committee and have now been reported to the house for discussion, we are told: "Oh, well, those estimates have been discussed at great length and you are holding up item No. 1".

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: I did not say that, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: With all due respect to my genial friend across the way, I say that he cannot have it both ways.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, or a question of privilege, may I say that I did not say that at all. I said that you could have the widest discussion on the item here. What I said was that this charge that we are trying to stop discussion was ridiculous because not only is the matter being discussed here but it was also discussed in the committee.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
The charge is not so ridiculous as the house leader would lead us to believe, Mr. Chairman. The minister said a moment ago that it is not the practice to hold up item No. 1. I say to him now that the former administration on more than one occasion held up item No. 1, not indefinitely but in order to give consideration to the matter which was submitted to the house; that matter was that the minister should hold up this item of his estimates until the government could report on winter work, until he could discuss with his colleagues in the government what the position was with reference to this extremely important matter of winter work which is of interest to all of us on this side of the house.
What I am saying now is that there should be no objection to telling the house what the position is. What harm could there be if item No. 1 were allowed to stand? In so far as I am personally concerned-and I can speak only for myself-I am prepared to state that if item No. 1 stood I am almost willing to wager that the other items would go through very quickly. Then if anything were to take place between the time this item was allowed to stand and the time it was passed there would be an opportunity for discussion of matters concerning the important department over which the minister presides. My only purpose in rising was to draw to the attention of the committee and of the minister the fact that on more than one occasion item No. 1 has been allowed to stand in the past. It would strike me that it should stand again on this occasion.

Supply-Labour

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: I think it is obvious now, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of Public Works regrets the fact that he extended the hours of the house sittings to include Saturdays. However, this is what has impressed me more than anything. Here we have in office a government which has assured the Canadian people that from the month of June, come the month of July we would overcome the problem of unemployment; that we were past the peak; that we were over the hump. Those assurances were broadcast across the nation. We are now in the month of August and all we can read in the reports emanating from the Department of Labour is the age-old phraseology that there has been a decrease in the rate of increase as it affects our number of unemployed. The minister tells us that no legislation is to be introduced. He says in effect that we cannot before the end of the session expect that there will be introduced into this house any legislation that has any specific design-

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: -or bearing of any major consequence on the subject of unemployment.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: Oh, yes; the minister has said that. The minister was unwilling, only a few minutes ago, to have item No. 1 held over.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
The minister voted against the motion that the committee now rise. The minister insists that this house now ought to complete discussion of his department in its over-all phases; in other words, he insists that a discussion of the basic principle ought now to end. He says that he is unwilling to go to the cabinet and unwilling to say to the cabinet: My colleagues, the House of Commons is not satisfied; the House of Commons wants more definite assurance that aggressive measures are being taken to meet the situation of unemployment.
This attitude bears out what I said yesterday, namely that this government seems to have made up its mind that it is going to attempt to ride out the storm. That is a cruel position to take when we consider human values. I feel that it is a dangerous position to take when we consider economic values. This air of uncertainty that obtains in the whole economic field throughout Canada, from Newfoundland to Vancouver island, must be cleared.
The people of Canada must have an assurance that we have in office a government that is master of the situation. We have not that assurance yet. The workers of Canada, the investors of Canada and the commercial
interests of Canada are faced with this feeling of uncertainty and that is our major handicap now. That is the major cause of unemployment today. This government feels that it can with platitudes restore prosperity. It feels that it is unnecessary to meet the situation head on with an air of aggressiveness which would involve legislation and which would involve this parliament. We are asked to accept these assurances. We had those assurances six months ago, Mr. Chairman. The statistics of the minister's department now show that the assurances of this government mean nothing. As far as the unemployed of Canada are concerned, these assurances are worthless. The unemployed last winter voted Conservative-let us make no mistake about it-because they had a certain confidence in this new regime.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: They still have.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: I remember, Mr. Chairman, that the former hon. member for Winnipeg North, Mr. Alistair Stewart, when the last parliament was in session, went home and lived with the unemployed in Winnipeg for one whole week. Then he came back to Ottawa and he brought back a report that worried me a little bit. He reported that half of the men in the line-up at the unemployment insurance offices were C.C.F. and the other half were Conservative. I failed to understand it. He said, "They are optimistic; they have a blind faith in this government". Those people today, six months later, no longer have that blind faith. Today they are filled with disillusionment.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: That's what you say.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
They now realize the truth about this government. They are not taking the minister at his word today. The minister is assuring us that the government need not introduce any legislation. In effect that is what he is doing. He is saying that the cabinet need not ask parliament to consider deliberate moves to solve this problem of unemployment. The minister has asked us today to accept in blind faith the assurances that were given six months ago and which have since been proven to be a hollow mockery to those who are unemployed; that is cruel indeed.
I have only one other remark to make and that concerns what the Minister of Public Works had to say when he attempted to tell us we ought to end our discussion now because this subject has been dealt with adequately.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: I did no such thing. The hon. member must not put words in my mouth like that.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY

I realize I must accept the statement of the minister. However, may I recall to the minister that only a few minutes ago he expressed a doubt as to the right of a lengthy discussion on item No. 1. If that is not an attempt to limit the debate on the subject of unemployment on this first item of the estimates of the Minister of Labour, then I do not know what he meant by that remark. That is today the most important subject facing the House of Commons of Canada, how to resolve this problem, and I am most amazed indeed that the Minister of Public Works, of all people, feels that a day and a half is overdoing things.
I believe the Minister of Labour will agree that this is the major problem facing his government now. I do not believe the minister can cite one other problem that haunts him and his colleagues in the cabinet as much as does the worry about unemployment. I am willing to give him credit, at least to that extent. However, I feel they are accepting advice from the wrong places. I feel they are accepting advice from those in Canada who believe a fairly heavy measure of unemployment is healthy for the Canadian economy. A large number of unemployed, it is believed, is one way in which you can keep organized labour in line-"in line" meaning as they see the line.
There are many people in Canada today who do not view with regret a fairly heavy dose of unemployment. We feel that these are the people who are advising the government to attempt to ride out the storm. May I remind the government that if they accept this advice their fate will be the same as was the fate of one other Conservative government, and they will be swept out in the holocaust that will occur on the Canadian economic scene.

speechtext: In order to straighten this out-

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: I am always serious about these questions. In order to straighten the matter out, I may say that it was not the former government which gave sanction to it. It was the treasury board.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: The hon. gentleman does accept my statement as accurate?

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: Yes, that the treasury board gave approval and the former government did not.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
It is quite evident from the figures just given by the minister, and from the report he tabled in the house on July 10,

that during the last seven months the unemployment insurance fund has been considerably reduced; in fact, that the unemployment insurance commission has in that period paid out $346 million. The fund which was close to $900 million over a year and a half ago is now reduced to something in the vicinity of $600 million and at this rate it is evident that within the next 12 to 18 months the fund will be depleted by at least 60 per cent.
In view of the serious situation, is the minister or is the government as a whole giving consideration to increasing the government's contribution to this fund which is regarded as security for the labour force of this country? It is evident that at the rate the fund has been depleted in the last year more substantial contributions by the federal government will be required.
If the minister does not want to answer that question, could he answer this simple one: Is it the intention of the government to introduce an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act to increase the government's contribution to the fund?

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: This government in a short space of time has gained the reputation in this country of giving consideration to all problems which are of importance to our people and certainly this is one such problem.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: I wonder if the minister, in view of the fact that he has just stated this government will give consideration to such a measure, could indicate whether there is any difference in his mind between giving consideration, giving active consideration and giving all sorts of other types of consideration, and whether he would indicate to the house what plans the government of which he is a member has for any kind of fulfilment of their primary objective which was said to be the maintenance of full employment. Has he any possible idea of how he is going to do it?

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: In answer to that question and in answer to a lot of other suggestions made in this debate I will say we have our own methods with respect to actions which have been taken and which will be taken. We have made recommendations on winter employment and most certainly we have not received any suggestion from any member of the opposition as to how that problem should be solved.

subtopic: GARIBALDI PARK, B.C.-INQUIRY AS TO TRANSFER OF RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: Would the minister indicate what are his solutions? He is one of those who were elected on false pretences as a result of that type of promise.

If the minister wants some suggestions, Mr. Chairman-he says he has not received any from this side of the house- I can assure him we have plenty of suggestions to make but we would prefer to make them in the proper constitutional fashion after the government has brought down its program. It seems to me that when we were elected, in my opinion unhappily for Canada, to oppose the government and the hon. gentlemen were, as I believe it will also turn out unhappily for the country, to conduct the government of this country, they were expected as a responsible government to bring in suggestions to deal with our problems and not to say "We have not heard any suggestions from the other side of the house and so we have no program". That is a preposterous attitude to take and I therefore renew my request to the house leader to have this item stand until the government has made up its mind and can bring down its program before this parliament so that all the elected representatives of the people can debate it.

I see that we do not get many answers to that question but could the minister give us one good reason why he does not want item one to stand? This government should try to do something to increase employment in Canada and what we want is not the dole; what we want is work for our unemployed.
If nothing is at present being done to prepare for next winter the load will once again be carried by the municipal and provincial authorities. Thousands and thousands of unemployed are being carried today who are not receiving any benefits because the municipalities have to give them food and they have to pay their rents and, after all, the provincial governments reimburse the municipalities for part of their expenditures in that connection. If we keep on this way many thousands of people will not work during this summer and so they will have no stamps for next winter and will again have to be carried by municipalities which have no means with which to look after them.
The only thing we want to know is whether the government has a policy. We want to know if the Minister of Labour has done something to create work for next winter. I know the Minister of Public Works has a public works program but it is not extensive enough to take care of all the unemployed. What is the Minister of Labour going to do because he is the one responsible for the situation? It is too bad that it happens to be he who is in charge at the present time but
Supply-Labour
it is his responsibility and he and the other members of the cabinet must find the means to solve the problem.
We are asking why will the minister not stand item No. 1. We will pass the rest today and when he has had a chance to discuss the matter with the other members of the cabinet and can come before the house during this session with a program for next winter, then we can deal with item No. 1. Up to now we know nothing; in fact I really think the minister does not know himself what he intends to do and that is not a proper way in which to administer a country, especially in a crisis such as that through which we are passing at the present time.

I wonder if I might ask
the minister two questions? Could he tell the house of the number of unemployed in 1956 and the number of new Canadians who have come to Canada since that time?
That does not solve the problem.

I do not have those figures
available.

I cannot allow those questions to pass unnoticed. Their indication is very very clear and it is that immigration is responsible for the level of unemployment. The member ought to know if he does not know-
Mr. Chairman, I can talk for myself.

-that the economic policies of the Canadian government are responsible for unemployment. Several years ago the Canadian Congress of Labour undertook a research program to find out to what extent immigration was responsible for our levels of unemployment and the report indicated very clearly that there was as much for as against the proposition of blaming immigration for unemployment. I hope that this is not an old Tory reaction coming to the fore which we thought had-as in fact the hon. member for Kootenay West said this morning -disappeared from Canada many many long years ago. I refer, of course, to the idea that the newcomers to our country are responsible for the ills which appear on the Canadian scene.
I am not yet convinced that immigration as such is responsible for unemployment and it is very wrong for this government to attempt, even through the mouth of a backbencher, to wash its hands of its responsibilities and to say it is the immigrants the Liberals let in who are responsible for our unemployment difficulties in Canada. I feel we are very right in our demand at the present time that the government should let

Supply-Labour
the Canadian people know what are its plans to meet the problems of the unemployment in Canada, not only winter unemployment but summer unemployment as well. We cannot afford to allow this item to go through and the government go off on its holidays several weeks hence, and let nature take its course and, maybe, end up by having a disaster happen in Canada next winter.
Shall the item carry?

No, I do not think I can let the aspersion made by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek pass in the way it has passed up to now, because I had the primary responsibility under the previous administration for quite some time for the immigration program, and I was accused by many members of the present government-and I am not talking now about their supporters-of having too small an immigration program. If they now think they are going to get away with blaming unemployment on the immigration program of the previous government, they have another think coming. I recall that many hon. members spoke on this matter, not least the present Prime Minister, who, speaking to the ethnic press association a few days before the election in June 1957, said we could have a 4 per cent increase per year if we had his government in office. The first thing they did after they came into office was to stop immigration. If they think they can get away with blaming unemployment on immigration they are mistaken, and I ask the minister: does he blame the present unemployment situation on immigration?

No, Mr. Chairman, I certainly do not, and I want to say that the last two speeches are purely partizan speeches and an attempt to make a difference between hon. members of this committee, as regards immigration-
I cannot let that pass, either. I did not bring up this subject.
Who did?
It was brought up by a supporter of the minister who was attempting, by innuendo, to cast aspersions-
He never drew conclusions.
The hon. and noisy member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot had better go to the public accounts committee if he wants to find out how to ask questions which contain more than the answers.

Order.
I think the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has got off the subject, which

deals with general administration. It is true the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek brought the question into the ring, but I think we should defer any further comments on it.
I quite agree, Mr. Chairman.

I think I am quite capable of answering for myself. I brought this question up for a reason, because I think you would find that the figures are very much the same as they were. If you add the unemployment figure in 1956 to the immigration figure since that date I would say the figure would be very much the same as the total unemployment today, and I say that this government has done a fine job in keeping employment to that level. I do not think the government is denying that unemployment has increased and that it will present a problem, but I have confidence, and so have the people of Canada, that our government has this problem under consideration and will do all that possibly can be done to remedy it.
Canada is not the only country which is facing this problem, and nothing is to be gained by members of the committee on my right repeating themselves time after time in order to make a political issue out of it. I think the people of Canada will realize what they are doing. This is a problem which the government appreciates, and the government intends to do something about it.

The hon. member talks about political issues. He did not have much thought of political issues when the Conservative party was trying to oust the Liberal party from office and when they dragged not only the poor unemployed, but every other political issue in the country into it. He does not have much thought now as to all the promises they gave, promises which they had no intention of keeping. The main promise was that there would be full employment for the working classes. There was no intention of keeping that because the government does not know how to keep that sort of promise. The hon. member who says we are talking politics with regard to this kind of thing has only to look back, not too long ago, to the election before last and see who dragged politics into everything and degraded the word politics in this country by making irresponsible promises which they had no intention of keeping.
Shall the item carry?
Mr. Chairman, coming back to the question which was put forward by the hon. member who spoke a while ago-

Order.

The Acling Chairman (Mr. Chown): I think a certain amount of latitude was allowed on that occasion which should not have been allowed. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was allowed to make a comment on it, but I think I will now rule that any further discussion on immigration as related to this item is out of order.

I find that very funny, Mr. Chairman, because you cannot read my thoughts, and I did not wish to speak on immigration at all, but on unemployment, which is part of this vote. When the hon. member who has spoken from my left tells us that we are making politics out of unemployment he is trying to say that members of this committee have no right to say here what they think to be right.
No such thing.

I do not think that any member of this committee has the right to tell another member what he should say or what he should not say, and the hon. member will have to learn in time that every member has an equal right here to say whatever he thinks fit. If the hon. member had been here at that time he would have heard the Minister of Labour in 1955 criticizing the government with regard to unemployment, and he was one of the harshest critics at that time.
The present Prime Minister also in 1955 used to criticize the government continually in a very severe fashion. The same thing is true with regard to the hon. member for Hamilton West who, I believe, was the opposition's official critic at the time. She, also, was very harsh in her criticisms of the government of that day. Now they want to stop us from criticizing government which has no policy whatever and which cannot even advise the committee what it intends to do with regard to next winter. I think that is out of place, and if I had been prevented from saying this I would have raised a question of privilege because we have the right to say what we think on these matters as well as any other members of this committee.

I notice that the minister has many excellent advisers with him. They are some of the most highly educated men in the country in the field of economics and in other related fields, and I know that the minister pays very close attention to any advice he receives from them. Is the minister able to inform the house as to what reasons his advisers gave him as to why we have this exceptionally high level of ununemployment in Canada at the present time, and what measures they are recommending
Supply-Labour
to him to overcome this problem. Why do we have this high level of unemployment?

In answer to that, I have been advised by the officials of my department in comparing last year's conditions with the conditions this year, that last year the economy was declining to a marked degree. In comparison, this year the economy is on the upswing at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the minister for that revealing statement of his to the effect that last year the economy was on the downgrade and this year it is on the upgrade, although this year we have twice as many unemployed as last year. Would the minister elucidate a bit on that point?
I must frankly admit that at the beginning of last year there were fewer people unemployed than there were at the beginning of this year.
Mr. Chairman, does the minister have unemployment figures for 1954?
I do not have them with me, Mr. Chairman.

At any rate it is safe to assume that the figure would be three or four times less than the present figure. I should like to place on the record some suggestions made in 1954 by the present Minister of National Defence which in light of the present attitude of the government can only be considered as strange. I refer to the French edition of Hansard, volume II, for the first session 1953-54, February 17, 1954, as found at page 2319 and following pages. I have the French translation of the remarks made on that occasion by the present Minister of National Defence who was then the private hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich at a time when unemployment was far below the level it has reached today and I invite hon. members to listen to what he said at that time:
(Translation) :
"Press reports of the last few days indicated that two battalions will be coming back from Korea very shortly. Approximately 50 per cent of the time-expired men take their discharge. They have done their period of service. Some feel they would like to take on army service as a permanent career. Others feel that they have done their duty by serving for the period of their contract, and they take their discharge.
"I should like to throw out the suggestion that some arrangement should be made whereby men are not released during these periods when there is the greatest seasonal unemployment".
The minister even went so far as to ask the government not to respect its obligation of

Supply-Labour
discharging the soldiers in Korea, even though they were entitled to discharge.
To continue the quotation:
"It seems to me it would not be very difficult for the services to provide some system of, shall we say, vocational training, to tide over that period when a man upon release will go out only to find that, owing to this seasonal unemployment, there is no prospect of finding a job''.
What's wrong with that?

If it's our friends from Quebec who want to know what's wrong with it, just let them listen to the rest of the quotation:
"Earlier this session I called attention to the fact that there was a shortage of reserves for our armed forces. In my speech last December I quoted at some length statements made by General Gruenther, supreme commander of NATO forces. I am not going to repeat his statements again except to quote a few lines from a speech made by General Gruenther at Copenhagen, when he was addressing United Nations commanders. He said: The creation of adequate reserve forces means that a large proportion of NATO manpower will have to devote a considerable time each year to reserve training. That is inconvenient for the individual concerned and of course it tends to create economic strains.
"It is inconvenient to the individual concerned if he has to do his reserve army or naval training at a time when he is fully employed, but it is not such a great inconvenience to him if his reserve training can take place at a time when he is not employed, owing to the seasonal nature of his employment.
"I would suggest ..."
Remember it is the Minister of National Defence who is speaking.
"-that those men who are periodically laid off because of the seasonal nature of their employment . . . might be provided with army and navy training at that time".
Let this not go unheeded by my good friends from the province of Quebec.
What does that mean?

"-and who have not become established with the security of their own homes to which they can go when unemployed".
I would like the members from the province of Quebec to listen carefully to what follows: "I would suggest that the extension of reserve naval training for fishermen is a line which might well be investigated by the Minister of Labour or by the committee on industrial relations when they consider this question of seasonal unemployment".
I ask my friends from Quebec to bear in mind that utterance of the Minister of National Defence, and to say here and now whether they endorse what he said at a time when he was a private member, and when unemployment was almost unknown in Canada.
Ignoramus!

"The same sort of thing applies with regard to-young men who are employed in the logging camps".
Now, if any members from Quebec have such young men in their ridings and if they are prepared to accept the statement made by the minister when he was a private member, let them rise and say so.
Either he was not in earnest, or else he was trying to get votes from the advocates of compulsory military service. Considering that we now have three or four times more unemployed, the minister's statement in 1954 ought to be all the more valid today.
I would ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) if he has the intention-and I would call it an ill-advised intention-of following the advice of the Minister of National Defence.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, I am far from happy yet with this bland assurance of the minister about the advice he received from his senior officials. A few moments ago he said that last year the economy was on the downgrade and this year it is on the upgrade. I should like the minister to inform us what evidence he has to support an assurance of that kind. The reports I have seen as to net profits of Canadian corporations, total Canadian production, total income of agriculture and net and real income of labour do not lead me to take an optimistic view of the present condition of our economy and on the basis of those reports I fail to see on what the minister's statement could be founded. I agree that in the field of housing there has been an upturn and an expansion but I should like the minister to indicate what is the basis of the assurance that the economy is on the upgrade this year which leads one by implication to the conclusion that we might hope to see some relief from the problem of unemployment.
On June 17 the Minister of Finance forecast optimistically an increase of 2 per cent but we have since learned that his assumption was based on no solid foundation. The Minister of Labour now tells us that his advisers inform him that our economy is on the upgrade and therefore, by implication, unemployment will cease to be a serious problem. Exactly what is the basis of the minister's assurance?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Shall the item
carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. I do not believe the minister can get away with a bland statement to the effect that the economy is on the upgrade without producing evidence concerning the foundation of that assurance.
Just keep right on talking.
All these men sitting in the gallery are costing the taxpayers a lot of money.
Who is costing the taxpayers money?
Mr. Chairman, on the problem of unemployment-
You will talk yourself out of the place.

May I assure the whip of the government that on the problem of unemployment I will keep talking until the snow comes. If this government thinks that having half a million or a million unemployed is something funny; that their summer holidays are more important than attending to the grocery bills and the mortgage bills of the unemployed, they have another guess coming and four years hence organized labour is going to throw them out. I repeat in all seriousness, Mr. Chairman, that the minister ought to account for his statement that the economy this year is on the upgrade. We cannot accept it simply as a statement.

One of the best indicators is the fact that registrations at our national employment service offices were on the increase as of August last year, but we have shown that there is a steady decline week by week in the registrations at our national employment services offices in recent weeks and although the dominion bureau of statistics figure for mid-July is not available yet-it has not been issued

I venture to predict that on the basis of the national employment service figure of 365,440 on August 7, there will be a very appreciable decrease in the D.B.S. figure for mid-July and even more so in the figure which will come out for mid-August.

If the minister should be wrong in that statement of his it would be simply disastrous because, after all, there is nothing new about unemployment figures declining in the month of May and a little less unemployment in June, a little less in July and even less in August. The minister knows
Supply-Labour
that in the summer months the berries have to be picked, the potatoes have to be planted and harvested, the tobacco has to be reaped and so on from one end of Canada to the other. There always is a decline in unemployment in the summer months. I am not very impressed either with this fantastic phrase, as I said before, that there is a decrease in the rate of the increase. I do believe honestly that a medal ought to be awarded to whatever civil servant first invented that phrase in reporting on the state of unemployment in Canada.
The minister's reply meant absolutely nothing, Mr. Chairman. The fact remains that in August we had twice as many unemployed as we had a year ago. The minister says that a year ago our economy was on the downgrade. He says that this year it is on the upgrade. We have twice as many unemployed. The minister has a bit of reconciliation to do. I believe that when he says the economy is on the upgrade he ought to have something more substantial to back up the statement than simply saying, well we are in the summertime and there is less unemployment than there was in the middle of winter.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I see the Prime Minister has come into the house. This is the second time that I have risen to speak on item No. 1, and to speak not at length but as briefly as I can. When I saw him come in I thought I should say briefly to him what has been taking place in his absence. Perhaps he has been listening.
He knows.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
But, in any event, I would like to make an appeal to him. The point is this, Mr. Chairman. In the discussion of item No. 1 there has been a demand from this side of the house as well as from the C.C.F. corner that this item be allowed to stand until some statement is made by the minister concerning the problem of unemployment during the winter months. The minister quite properly has said that the matter is one which is to receive the consideration of the government because of the representations which have been made by the various municipalities. He felt that he could not make a statement until he had an opportunity to discuss the matter with his cabinet colleagues and, as I said, there is no fault to be found with that statement. But I am wondering- and I am appealing to the Prime Minister on this basis-whether this item should not be allowed to stand until some consideration be given to those representations and a statement made in the house.
I am informed, and I believe that such was the case on former occasions. I do know of

Supply-Labour
more than one instance when the first item of the minister's estimates stood until some further consideration could be given to certain matters. I appealed earlier to the leader of the house and suggested to him that if the item were allowed to stand I was sure there would be no difficulty in so far as the remaining items were concerned.
My only reason in rising when I saw the Prime Minister come in was that I felt-as did many hon. members on this side of the house-that it would be taking the house in its confidence if the government was to stand this item so that at a later date it might report on those representations and say what ones, if any of them, could be implemented during the time that parliament will be in recess. I am sure the Prime Minister would not want to do otherwise than to give this suggestion, which is made in all sincerity, due consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I can understand the sincerity with which the contribution has been made, but I fail to see that there is any necessity to hold up this item. The minister intends to make further statements and in particular when the unemployment insurance item is before the committee. If, in the circumstances, the hon. gentlemen opposite do not feel that the minister's statement is what they want, I am not going to alter in any way, or suggest an alteration in, the stand that has been taken.
The minister is prepared to answer any question. If the presentations are of such benefit as indicated-and I am sure they are- the minister will naturally want to take them under advisement and consideration. That, however, does not mean that item No. 1 needs to be held up indefinitely.
I must say that as long as hon. gentlemen opposite have a contribution to make I am sure they will continue to discuss item No. 1; but to say to the minister and to the government that we will not pass item No. 1 unless certain statements are made and consideration given to the representations that we have to offer is a perfectly proper stand for the opposition to take; but the taking of that stand is not completely conducive to that spirit that one would expect would prevail in a matter as important as this.
I am always anxious to see the opposition given every opportunity. I must say that throughout this session, as I listen to the contributions that are made, I think of other days when we used to be cut off most peremptorily if we endeavoured to secure information. But that is far from our attitude. As long as questions are asked they will be answered no matter how long it takes. I want to see this debated to the limit. If hon.

gentlemen opposite feel that they have representations that are helpful I am sure the longer we are on this particular item the more beneficial it will be to give our consideration to those questions in order to meet the problem particularly of winter employment which, I think, is the reason for the request that this item be held up.
There are many more items upon which hon. gentlemen can speak. I for one would not want to enter into any arrangement by which an item would be held conditional upon certain eventualities taking place. Hon. gentlemen have their representations to make continually. Nothing is more helpful than any additional suggestions they have, even though they did not bring them into effect when they had the power to do so. Nonetheless, in the retrospect of solitude, beneficial results often follow. No doubt they have suggestions and I welcome them. This is a troublesome problem. If the item under which a general discussion could take place is now before the committee, I am sure the hon. member for Laurier would not expect me to suggest, as long as beneficial ideas are forthcoming, that this item should in any way be set aside and removed from the field of immediate discussion. I say that with great respect for his suggestion. I know that the suggestion was made with a sincere desire to be helpful. My answer to him is in the same spirit.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I thank the Prime Minister for his sincerity of approach to the suggestion I made. I should not like him to be under a misapprehension as to what I had suggested. I am afraid that in his reply he indicated that he was under a misapprehension. I did not ask that the item be held up indefinitely.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
In his reply the Prime Minister created the impression that the item be held up indefinitely. That was not my suggestion; far from it. I do not think a request of that nature would be a proper one and I tell the Prime Minister that immediately. That is not my request and I am sure it is not the request of those of us who sit on this side of the house. The only request made was that it be held up so that we might be given the opportunity of hearing the minister with reference to the program for winter employment. The Prime Minister has said, "What suggestions have you to offer? If you have any suggestions, here we are and we will listen to them". The opposition has been saying-and I simply repeat and reiterate

it-that is the responsibility of the government and that it is not the responsibility of the opposition.
Oh, oh.
That statement fairly well answers the earlier request.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That is exactly the attitude which the former leader of the opposition took when he sat on this side of the house, namely that the responsibility lay over there on the government side and not on this side of the house. That is why we say to him, with all due respect, that it seems to us that we should be entitled to know before we rise what is the program that is envisaged during the next few months and what is the program envisaged for winter employment. The Prime Minister seemed also to be of the opinion that an attempt was being made to dictate to the government. From what I said previously and from what I am saying now surely there is not the slightest intention of any such attempt. On the contrary, I am making a request and it seems to me to be a reasonable request. If the Prime Minister feels that it is not a reasonable request or if the government feels that it is not a reasonable request, that is all right. I have made the request; they have considered it; they have turned it down. That is fine. But the request is made in that light and in the circumstances that I have stated.
I do not know whether or not I understood the Prime Minister properly but I thought I heard him say that there would be an opportunity for further discussion of this matter under item 179, at which time the minister would make a statement. Was my understanding correct and is it the intention of the minister on item 179 to make a statement about the winter employment program?

At the outset, Mr. Chairman, I said that I would make a statement on unemployment on item 179 but evidently that procedure was not acceptable to the members of the opposition. Since then we have not been able to get down to that item so that I could make that statement.

May I just say a word, Mr. Chairman, since I was the one-the hon. member for Laurier was not in the committee at the time-who made the first request to the house leader. 1 should just like to recall what the circumstances were. I had asked the minister-and I think I had done so with great consideration-whether he could give us a report on the conference on winter employment which was held some three or four weeks ago. The minister replied-and I at once agreed quite readily
Supply-Labour
-that he had not had an opportunity of discussing the results of the conference with his colleagues and it would not be proper for him to give a statement to the house on that conference until he had discussed it with his colleagues. We in our party on this side of the house accepted that position at once as a proper one and did not quarrel with the minister at all. Then I rose and, in as considerate terms as I could, asked the house leader whether in those circumstances he would not allow item No. 1 to stand until the government had had a chance to consider its position and the minister could give this report to us with the weight of the government behind it. That is all we have asked for at any time. The request was made in order that we should have the government's position stated to us so that it could be debated.
I recall that on many occasions, when we were sitting on the treasury benches, situations of that kind arose when members of the opposition, for one reason or another, asked for information that was not immediately available and items were held up by ministers until the information could be obtained and other items were gone on with. That is all that our request was, namely that instead of dealing with this item we go on and deal with the rest of the items of the department, and that it be allowed to stand until the government had had an opportunity to consider the results of this conference and report to us.

All I want to say before we pass this item is this, Mr. Chairman; and I can assure the house that we are now prepared to end our part in the discussion on this item. We attempted to find out from the minister what, in the opinion of the government, was the cause of the seriously high number of unemployed in Canada. The minister in effect said that last year the economy was on the downgrade and that this year the economy is on the upgrade. That is the only explanation he had to offer as to why this year in the month of August we had twice as many unemployed as we had a year ago. That statement is entirely unacceptable as an explanation from a responsible minister of labour.
Then we further asked what are the intentions of the government not only in relation to a winter employment program but with regard to solving the problem. How does this government propose to obtain the objective of full employment which, I am sure, all members of this government share. We received no reply whatsoever on that score, except an indication of a reply in the comments of the Prime Minister, when he

Supply-Labour
assured us that this matter was a responsibility of the government. As we pointed out earlier, we had that assurance six months ago from one end of Canada to another. The statistics now show that that assurance did not mean a thing in that unemployment is at an exceptionally high level for this season of the year. We expressed our dissatisfaction at this time that this parliament is again willing to shelve its responsibility and to place its faith completely and blindly in the government, thinking that the government is going to solve this problem and that consultation and action on the part of parliament will not be necessary.
We maintain that this problem is not going to be met without the advice and action of the House of Commons of Canada. We feel that it is playing with human lives, it is playing with the welfare of the Canadian economy, to put such blind confidence in the members of the government in connection with this serious problem.

I am sure that the Prime Minister recalls those words which he addressed to the previous administration when he said that, day after day, week after week, they were determined not to supply the opposition with information. Just a while ago he stated that the Minister of Labour was prepared to answer any questions addressed to him. I have a simple question. Can the Minister of Labour advise this committee if positive recommendations have been offered to him by the provincial-federal conference which took place in Ottawa a few weeks ago in connection with winter unemployment?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. It was not entirely a provincial-federal conference. It was a conference in which many organizations participated and gave their thoughts and ideas to us. There are some very good suggestions in that report, some suggestions that can be put into effect immediately and others on a long-term basis. As I said, it will be submitted for action, so that the government can segregate those that can be put into effect immediately for immediate results, and those that can be brought into effect to give results on a long-term basis.

Item agreed to.
172.	Annuities Act-administration, $1,178,839.

Might I ask the minister if he can report on the progress that has been made in connection with a certain matter concerning employees who change from one employer to another? What I have in mind is that, in effect, the annuities branch may become the means of establishing a transferable pension plan. Are more pension plans

entering the annuities branch? We know there are many industrial enterprises in Canada who, upon setting up pension plans, have agreed with the unions that those pension funds shall be invested in the annuities branch of the federal government. If an employee moves and can find a new employer who also has his pension plan under the annuities branch, then in effect that employee has a transferable pension plan or what is sometimes called a portable pension plan. Are more pension funds being invested in the annuities branch of the Department of Labour or has the number become less?

The government administers its own pensions, and so far as other pensions are concerned or the act of transferring from one to the other, that matter has been given study but to date no action has been taken and no changes have been made.

I do not think the minister realized what I was saying. I will use an example of which I am aware. The Brack-man-Ker Milling Company in New Westminster has a pension plan. These funds, to which the employer and the employee contribute, are invested and there is purchased for the individual concerned an annuity with the federal government annuities branch of the Department of Labour. Now, an employee leaving the employment of Brackman-Ker Milling Company and entering the employ of another industry anywhere else in Canada could, in effect, have what is often described in Canada as a portable pension plan if he could find another enterprise whose pension funds were also invested in the annuities branch of the Department of Labour.
I was asking the minister if he was aware of either an increase in the number of industrial enterprises who have invested their pension funds in the annuities branch, or a decrease?

As I understand the hon. member's question, it is this: If a person works for one firm which has a group plan in which he participates, and leaves the employment of this particular company to find employment with another one which has also a government annuity plan, then can a transfer be made? I am advised that it is not transferable but remains as an annuity in the firm for which he has worked up to $120 a year. It is not redeemable until the age of retirement.
Is the minister now able to advise whether there are more companies using the facilities of the annuities branch than there were a year ago?
The total number of individual contracts issued is 182,147. In 1957, there were 5,937 individual contracts issued and in 1958, 6,701, or an increase of approximately 800.

I am sure the minister agrees that a transferable pension plan for the workers of Canada is a desirable thing, and that it would be of immense advantage not only to Canadian employees but also to Canadian employers in that it would enable the discrimination that presently exists against older workers to be eliminated. Does the minister not consider that the annuities branch might well explore this field, and might profitably devote a little of its publicity to the possibilities that exist in the annuities branch for the working people of Canada? I realize that today there are some very high priced insurance men in Canada going from one industrial enterprise to another and spending a lot of their time in one union office after another. They do their best to persuade the union offices and the executives of Canadian enterprises to invest their pension plan funds in company A, B, C or whatever else it may be. However, these people who work in the interests of these insurance companies will never bother to inform either the union officials or the corporation executives of the existence of the annuities branch of the Department of Labour.
Does the minister not agree that a very useful service might be performed for the welfare of the working people if the annuities branch made both employers and union organizations aware of the possibilities of establishing a transferable pension plan through advantage being taken by investing pension funds in the annuities branch?

There is a problem of investment where the employer and the employed contribute and there seems to be a difficulty in bringing about any such change. However, I will look into the situation and see what are the possibilities.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister some anomalies which have resulted from the method by which prevailing rates are determined by his officials.
I understand that the Department of Labour has officials in certain branches whose duty it is to take samplings of prevailing rates
Supply-Labour
in certain areas and that these rates are used as a basis for the wages paid to people employed by the federal government as casual labourers, people who are employed seasonally and in some cases as full-time workers. In 1939 when the United States government decided to build bases in Newfoundland we came up against this problem. The wage scale for various crafts paid by the United States government were far in excess, sometimes even double those paid locally and while the U.S. government was quite willing to pay the same rates to Newfoundland employees, the commission of government at that time stepped in and set up an arbitrary scale of wages to be paid to Newfoundlanders working at the U.S. bases. We therefore had the situation where Newfoundlanders and United States citizens would be working on the same job, side by side, doing exactly the same work, with the United States citizen getting twice and three times as much as the local labourer.
After confederation we thought we had got rid of this sort of thing but it has only recently come to our attention that this same thing is still being practised as a result of the policy of the fixing of local rates by the Department of Labour. As a result we get a situation such as the one with respect to the hydrographic service which for the past two or three years has conducted surveys for the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. In this case two small boats of about 40 feet in size have been working in my own riding and it has come to my attention that these two boats, of exactly the same size and doing exactly the same work, are being paid different rates because the crew of one was recruited in Nova Scotia while the crew of the other was recruited in Newfoundland. The difference in the rates is fairly substantial and I think that is a very serious inequity which should be corrected.
As a result of this practice officials employed by the Department of Transport such as assistant lighthouse keepers, and assistant foglamp keepers are suffering from very tremendous inequities as a result of this policy. So much so that the assistant keeper who has exactly the same duties as the man in charge and who has exactly the same hours of work -the only difference in their responsibilities being the sending in of a monthly report-gets sometimes even less than half the salary of the keeper. In addition to this the keeper gets two or three weeks' holiday with pay and has other advantages, such as the provision of his coal, which are not available to the assistant keepers. This is a very serious matter which should be corrected. I do not know the full answer but personally I believe

Supply-Labour
this government should adhere to the policy laid down by the parliament several years ago when we agreed to the principle of equal pay for equal work in respect of women. I do not see why the same principle should not apply to men, particularly when government employees are involved. People employed by the federal government on identical jobs are certainly entitled to get exactly the same pay. The federal government is a very peculiar employer if it puts into effect one set of rates for Canadians in one part of the country and another set of rates into effect for Canadians in another part of the country even though they do exactly the same work.
The same policy is also in effect outside of Canada for in our embassies we employ local labour subject to the conditions I have outlined above. I happened to be in South America and I found that we had stenographers and secretaries in our embassies who had gone down there from Canada and were being paid wonderful salaries, in addition to which they received cost of living allowances because they were away from home which were up in the thousands while in the same embassies South American citizens were employed at much lower rates who were even more capable than our own people, people who could speak three or four languages. I know of one girl in particular who was a competent stenographer and who was fluent in four languages yet, simply because she was a citizen of that country, she was getting less than a quarter of what we were paying our own people. I think this gives Canada a very bad name and certainly does not enhance our prestige in foreign countries. I hope the minister will take an interest in this question and will do something to straighten it out as quickly as possible.
I think part of the trouble is that too small a sample is taken and that if we must have this sampling procedure, and if we cannot go the whole-hog, then we should at least set up one set of prevailing rates for the maritimes, another for central Canada and another for the west. There certainly should not be such a wide discrepancy in the rates for Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as obtains at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct the attention of the minister for a few minutes to the current dissatisfaction that exists in the province of Newfoundland concerning the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act. His attention has already been called to this question by other hon. members from that province who have participated in this debate and also indeed this was accomplished in discussions I have held with the minister on previous occasions.
The dissatisfaction arises from two sources. The first is that claims requiring processing have to be sent from Newfoundland to Moncton, New Brunswick. This sometimes results

Supply-Labour
in delays which are caused by weather conditions involving slowness of delivery of mail and so on. The other factor relates to the general geographic conditions that obtain in the province of Newfoundland. I would point out, for instance, that the total area of Newfoundland is approximately 153,000 square miles and a population of 425,000 people is sparsely scattered over this vast area. This creates difficulties when one takes into consideration the fact that the unemployment insurance commission has only three offices in the entire province.
It has been suggested that the office in St. John's is the largest in the Atlantic region. I urge the minister and his officials to give consideration to effecting a change in the administration of the act under which it would be possible for claims to be finalized in St. John's without having to be referred to Moncton. This would considerably speed up the processing of claims.
Another question raised by hon. members from Newfoundland concerned a request that consideration be given to sending more men into the field to process claims all over Newfoundland and indeed on the coast of Labrador in order that fishermen and loggers will not have to suffer undue delay in receiving unemployment insurance payments. This is of considerable importance to a province that has a serious seasonal unemployment problem. I would remind the minister that many large national companies including banks, insurance companies and even the Canadian National Railways have seen the wisdom of setting up a special Newfoundland region because the problems of the province are not directly related to those of the maritime provinces and in fact are quite different from the point of view of geography, the economy and so forth.
In closing I would also ask the minister and his officials to give consideration to the erection of a new building in St. John's to house the huge staff of the unemployment insurance office. As the officials are probably aware the staff is presently housed in a temporary building erected by the Canadian navy during world war II. I submit that these quarters are most unsatisfactory and not conducive to the proper processing of claims. I ask the minister and his officials to give serious consideration to these recommendations.

Mr. Chairman, as an hon. member who represents a tobacco producing area I wish to bring to the attention of the minister and the committee what appears to be a tobacco job racket that flourishes at this time of year. I regret to have to say this racket appears to operate from certain

centres in the province of Quebec. Apparently these operators advertise that they can furnish jobs in the tobacco areas of Ontario for the harvesting of the tobacco crop. Prospective workers are required to pay a certain sum of money for transportation to the area. Unfortunately upon their arrival in the tobacco-producing areas of Ontario those individuals who have sought employment find jobs are not available and they are among the many hundreds of people seeking work. If they are lucky they may have sufficient money to get back home but if they have insufficient funds they are left stranded in those areas.
What I wish to suggest is that the national employment offices in Montreal and other areas of Quebec give wider publicity to this kind of labour racket which is carried on by a very few individuals. May I also suggest that persons seeking work in the harvesting of tobacco in Ontario should consult their unemployment insurance offices to ascertain if any jobs are available before going to the tobacco producing areas of that province.

Mr. Chairman, I also wish to say a few words about the unsatisfactory way in which the claims of Newfoundlanders for unemployment insurance are processed and administered. I wish to make it clear I am not criticizing the personnel of the department but in Newfoundland we have certain conditions that do not obtain in other parts of Canada and I think the Department of Labour should adjust itself to those conditions because certainly they have existed for thousands of years and are not going to adjust themselves to the Department of Labour.
There are many things that could be done to speed up the processing of unemployment insurance claims in Newfoundland. As I have travelled throughout the province I have had occasion to fill out forms for people not able to do it for themselves. While on the surface the forms appear fairly simple yet there is some confusion created by the fine print. In my experience in filling in forms I have been uncertain just how much information I should fill in on the form. I believe the forms could be simplified still more.
Another matter which considerably aggravates the situation relates to the date on which the form must be filled in. I believe for the purposes of the administration of the act the week begins on Monday and ends on Sunday. In many areas of Newfoundland there is slow mail service. In some areas delivery is only once a week, or ten days, and in winter it frequently is two weeks or even longer. A man filling in the form knows that the mail is coming at a certain date and

he will put the date on. The inherent honesty of those people compels them to put down that date. They could put a false date and everything would be all right, but because they put down the exact date when they make out the form, and that date does not conform to the date required by the department, when it gets in, after travelling eight or 10 days, to the unemployment office the clerk looks at the date and immediately says that the date is wrong and sends it all the way back to him again to be corrected. It takes perhaps another three or four weeks before it gets back to him and he has to wait for another mail and send it back again, and all because he was honest enough to put the right date on it.
Our people in the local office should be familiar enough with the conditions to know that in those outports when a fisherman particularly fills in one of those forms he is not going to work the day after and continue working for any lengthy period. I think the practice of returning forms to claimants for such a trivial cause is unnecessary and causes a lot of unnecessary annoyance.
Something more could be done to facilitate those claims if the clerks in the office would watch when the mail closes, because the mails for certain parts of Newfoundland close on a certain date and the claims that are being adjusted for that period should be in the mail on that date. If they are posted the day after, then they just lie in the post office for another week or 10 days until the mail comes again, and that is an unnecessary delay which could be corrected if the clerks were watching the closing of the mails.
I have often thought that the office in St. John's should be organized on a sort of district basis so that certain clerks would be dealing with claims coming from a certain part of the island and would have the responsibility of seeing that those claims got in the mail at the proper time in order that there would be no unnecessary delay.
Another cause of great annoyance-and again unnecessary annoyance-is the refusal or the failure of the office to reply to correspondence. Almost every letter I get complaining about delay in adjustment of claims states that the writer has written to the unemployment office two or three times. Sometimes they telegraph two or three times and have not had the courtesy of receiving a reply. That not only causes a great deal of annoyance but undermines confidence in the department itself. These things are unnecessary, Mr. Chairman, and I do hope the minister will take whatever steps are possible to have them corrected.
