Mr. Chairman, I just want to make some remarks because of the representations which were made by the hon. member for St. John's East and yesterday by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and last night also in respect of the Unemployment Insurance Act and by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. I must say that after all there has been a handicap in the operation of the unemployment insurance this year simply because it was our first experience with fishermen coming under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Most certainly it was expected that there would be some anomalies that through experience would have to be corrected as they were brought forward. I think that with one year's experience in this matter we shall see that some of these things are cleared up to the satisfaction of those who are the recipients of unemployment insurance.
Last night the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said that I would have no objection to the fact that it was the previous government that brought the fishermen under the act. I agree readily that that is so. I have no objection to that, but it was this government which brought forward legislation to give them an additional two months on a permanent basis and also an additional six weeks after that period for this year.
I have noted the representations made in this regard and most certainly we shall look into the situation to see how some of those anomalies can be rectified.
As to the Unemployment Insurance Act itself, I want to say to the committee that I have submitted certain suggestions to the unemployment insurance commission and suggestions, 1 might say, which reflect a major change in unemployment insurance, necessitating a great deal of study. Some of those recommendations were studied in the unemployment insurance advisory committee in the early part of July. They are convening again on August 19 to study the remainder of the suggestions, and I hope that when the recommendations are received from them I shall have the opportunity of getting the approval of the government and bringing them before parliament next session. I had hoped it might be this session but it certainly does not look as though that may be possible. I should like to see those amendments given thorough study and be referred to the industrial relations committee.
I said at the outset that I would make a statement on unemployment. Because of the continued debate we have had this afternoon I must admit at once that I have already given considerable information regarding the winter employment conference, which relates to this, and X have also

Supply-Labour
covered other aspects that have been raised as the debate progressed this afternoon. Generally speaking, I think the committee will agree that since becoming Minister of Labour I have dealt fully and frankly with the problem of unemployment. Possibly in doing so I have dealt with it in some instances with restrained optimism-
What does that mean?
It is optimism with some restraint. I have never made any attempt-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It means frankly but not fully.

I have never made any attempt at any time, I think, to lull this house as to the fullest extent of the problem which we have faced and we did face it last winter, and I think there is every likelihood that we are facing it now. But I would also say that this is a problem which this government faced in the past and faced firmly, and will face it as it comes before us again in the future.
I want to say at once, Mr. Chairman, that the government's firm and quick action last year in dealing with this unemployment last winter, resulted in keeping our economy much more firmly in balance than was the case in some other countries and perhaps much more so than was expected. I think the steps that were taken by the government, and above all the knowledge that the government was prepared to take steps, had a profound psychological effect in building up public confidence last winter. I found that as I travelled across this country, particularly last spring, and had the opportunity of visiting our offices and seeing what effect it did have, and I was heartened by what was being done.
What is the present situation? From the information at my disposal I would say that in the last couple of months there has been a considerable improvement in our general situation. This improvement has reflected itself in the fact that where a year ago unemployment was rising at a faster than seasonal rate, it is now declining at a faster than seasonal rate, and this is borne out by the economists of our department who did not, I must admit frankly, anticipate that this trend would take place at this time of the year.
In recent months we have seen the effects of the action taken by the government last fall. There was a tremendous upswing in domestic housing construction and a steady rise in retail sales. This may be traced directly to government action in pumping money into housing and in keeping up purchasing power with extended social

security payments, assistance to municipalities, in dealing with unemployment assistance to farmers and fishermen. These too have had their effect. Then there was the announcement by the government of its readiness to undertake large capital expansion projects such as Saskatchewan irrigation and maritime power. I think all of these things have been reflected in increased public confidence.
In regard to my own department, may I say that I was most pleased that the Leader of the Opposition was good enough yesterday to register interest in what we were doing about the situation. The extension of benefits during the winter and spring, of course, is familiar to all members of this house. The continuing emphasis on placement by the national employment service I have already mentioned. This will continue at an accelerated pace and has, I might say, begun to show an effect in recent months. Our winter employment campaign last winter was the most ambitious one ever undertaken by the department. This year we are asking for $150 thousand again. I would suggest to hon. members that the results of this campaign do not linger entirely in the realm of academic conjecture. I myself have seen evidence, as I mentioned earlier, of how this campaign was working out.
There is no need for me to refer to the winter employment conference because I think I have dealt with it to the fullest possible extent. The recommendations will be put before the cabinet for their consideration and action. We are taking this action. We propose to take more action as it becomes necessary. I can assure this house that we recognize our responsibility and that we will face up to it. We have done so in the past and we will do so in the future.
I just want to illustrate what I meant by the fact that there is a decline where there was an increase in our employment which is more than seasonal. The figure for registrations on July 10 this year stood at 83 per cent higher than for the same date last year. The figure for July 17 was 60 per cent higher than last year; and the figure for July 31 was only 45 per cent higher than last year. Since then we have noticed a continual drop in our registrations, a fact which indicates that there is a downward trend in unemployment whereas last year at the same period there was an upward trend. On the basis of these figures I say that there will be a considerable drop in the D.B.S. figures in mid-July. There is bound to be because the N.E.S. figures indicate that. Most certainly there will be a decrease in the D.B.S. figures for midAugust. That is all I wanted to say, Mr. Chairman.

There is just one question which I omitted to ask when I was on my feet earlier. Last night in his opening remarks the minister referred to the table appearing on page 2137 of Hansard with respect to the unemployment insurance fund. I think that table was placed there in reply to a question which I put on the order paper. I wonder whether the minister could bring us up to date by giving us the corresponding figures of contributions or payments for June and also for July, if they are available.
The last figures we have are for the month of June. I do not know what was shown on the table that was placed on Hansard. Was it for the end of May?
Yes.

The only additional group of figures we have is for the month of June. The contributions of employers and employees for June were $14,885,735.42; government, $2,972,973.64. Do you want the figures right across the page?
Yes.
Fines and penalties, $4,193.82; interest on investment and profit on sale of securities-
No. I do not think we need those figures. I should just like to have the contributions and the withdrawals or benefit payments.
The figure for ordinary benefit payments was $26,021,851.26; supplementary and seasonal, $10,941,005.65; or a total of $36,962,856.91.
I thank the minister.

Before this item passes there is one matter on which I should like to speak for just a moment and concerning which I should like to ask the minister a question. It has to do with the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act, particularly as it affects workers in the community of greater Windsor and in fact all the ridings in Essex county. For that matter, I think it also applies to many other ridings in which there is a fair percentage of workers engaged in the automobile industry. It is my understanding that this is a matter which the government inherited in that it concerns the administration of regulations which were in effect at the time this government came into office. It is a matter which I have discussed with the minister and for the benefit of our community I should like to have some assurance that it is receiving consideration from the government. I think it is of particular
57071-3-234
Supply-Labour
importance because of the fact that the automobile industry in this present recession has suffered a great deal more than has any other manufacturing industry. It is of particular concern to the people of my riding in that the greater percentage of the workers in the industrial area of Windsor are engaged in the automobile industry.
At the present time, as I understand it, benefits are derived under the act based upon the contributions made by the worker during the last immediately preceding 30 weeks of employment. We all know that because of the depressed condition of the automobile market the workers hours of employment were reduced during each working week. Their contributions, of course, have been reduced accordingly. Their benefits are reduced where their contributions have been thus reduced. That condition continued for a substantial period of time until finally in many instances lay-offs took place in the industry and the workers then, of course, applied for benefits under the act. The suggestion has been made that instead of benefits being based upon the contributions made during the last immediately preceding 30 weeks of a period of some 104 weeks, they be based upon an average over the period of 104 weeks. I should like to know whether the minister is giving that matter consideration and whether we may look for some relief.

I have had this matter referred to me by others who are interested, and I thank the hon. member for bringing it again to my attention. When the unemployment insurance advisory committee meets on August 19, that will be one of the problems with which they will be dealing at that time.
May I ask the hon. member for Essex West why he did not vote for the amendment to reduce the excise tax on automobiles when it was introduced a few weeks ago?

I am
afraid I have to rule that question out of order.

I have my eye on the
clock, as I see the minister has, too. I do not want to hold up his estimates. We have had some correspondence about the matter of decentralization where, in my opinion and perhaps the minister's opinion, it is justified, having regard to some of the views of the unemployment insurance commission that centralization is a very desirable thing in its administration. I have in mind the need, particularly in these times, of service at

Supply-Labour
Dryden and Atikokan. I do not want to pursue it. I do not even want the minister to reply at the moment, because he did write me about two weeks ago in a very informative way. However, I am serious about this, as he knows. I had some association with the treasury board and I am conscious of the desire to reduce administrative costs wherever it is possible. I believe the minister has been up in our territory and he knows that we have a very big area to cover, particularly in a winter such as the one we have gone through. The distance to be travelled can be from 150 miles to 300 miles for these individuals who have to deal with the unemployment insurance office. I think that is important. I feel that perhaps we are a little overstaffed at Fort William, and perhaps we could take one or two men from Kenora in order to serve Atikokan and Dryden. I am not asking for an increase in overhead, but I am asking for greater service to the individual who may be concerned.

Item agreed to.
Annuities Act-
571.	Administration-further amount required, $58,000.

I do not want to take very long, but I have a question to ask of the minister. I have been informed that when the amount does not exceed $10 per month the person concerned can get his money back. I was told this in the committee. If the amount exceeds $10 per month a man has to wait until he is sixty-five to get it. I have met people who because of ill health were unable to continue in their employment and were unable to find work for which they were fit. They could not get their contributions, which were around $12 a month, returned. I am wondering if the law could not be changed so that people could get their money returned up to a higher amount, especially at this time when there is hardship in Canada. Sometimes they want to start a small restaurant or other commercial enterprise, buy a truck to earn their living, and the only money on which they could lay their hands would be the money which is in these annuities. Would it be possible for the minister to study the matter to see if the amount could not be increased to $20 or $25 a month, so that these fellows could get their money back and start some new enterprise with this money?

Item agreed to.
573. Administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act, including expenditures incurred in connection with other duties and responsibilities assumed and carried out as required by the governor in council on the recommendation of the Minister of Labour in accordance with section 4 of the act-further amount required, $1,489,434.

I am sure this will only take a minute. Is the minister able to say whether or not he has considered opening more offices of the unemployment insurance commission in the urban areas or is his policy also one of centralization?

My policy is not one of centralization. Personally, I feel we should give as great a service as it is possible to give to those who need to use our offices. I am continually asking the commission to consider the establishment of offices, providing it is economical to establish them. In other words, there would have to be a sufficient number of people making use of that office. Most certainly we do not want an office in an isolated area where there is no business for it, so to speak. I believe that we should have as many offices as is necessary in order to give as good a service as we possibly can to the people of Canada.

I just ask the minister to look at the statistics, as I have done. I do not blame him, because I have had arguments with his predecessors about this very same problem. If he will look at the percentage of time spent by the staff of the Fort William office with reference to people from Atikokan, which is almost 100 miles away, I am sure he will feel that there could be some division of staff without any increase in public expenditure.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Will we continue with that business on Tuesday?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

I am not sure of that. The house would have to be prepared to take any of those on Tuesday and also possibly the second reading of the act to amend the Customs Act and the act to amend the trust companies and

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Can the minister give any indication as to when the Radio Act will come up.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I have already listed the resolution which precedes the act having to do with broadcasting.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to the order of the house passed on August 4.

Question
The following answer, deposited with the Clerk of the house, is printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

What grants were made to the hospitals of the province of Quebec under the national health program from 1948 to the 1st of June, 1957, for (a) construction: (b) hygiene, health services: (c) other hospital services?
Answer by: Hon. J. W. Monieith (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
(a) $22,798,003; (b) and (c) $26,178,303.
